newsitem.title: USA: Ill. governor hails dismissal of incinerator suit.
newsitem.headline: Ill. governor hails dismissal of incinerator suit.

text.p: Illinois Gov. Jim Edgar applauded a U.S. District Court ruling Friday dismissing a lawsuit filed by Foster Wheeler Corp contesting the loss of a state subsidy for a bond-financed incinerator in Robbins, Ill., that the company developed.
"We believe the repeal of the Retail Rate Act protected the environment and Illinois taxpayers from potentially billions of dollars in subsidies," said Eric Robinson, Edgar's spokesman.

Robinson had no comment on Foster Wheeler's announcement that it would appeal the dismissal in the U.S. Court of Appeals and is considering refiling its lawsuit in state court. The Clinton, N.J.-based company also said it will consider pursuing administrative remedies with the Illinois Commerce Commission.
Federal Judge James Zagel dismissed the lawsuit on the ground that the 11th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution precludes lawsuits against states dealing with public funds.

Edgar, along with commerce commission officials, were sued by Foster Wheeler, its Illinois subsidiaries and the village of Robbins in a lawsuit that charged the state's repeal in March of a 1987 state subsidy for incinerators violated several U.S. Constitutional provisions, including impairment of contract, equal protection and due process.
The subsidy contained in the Retail Rate Act had allowed incinerators to sell their electricity to utilities at a higher rate subsidized by the state.

"Our company has done an outstanding job in responding to the inducements offered by the state of Illinois when it enacted the Retail Rate Law in 1987," said Richard Swift, Foster Wheeler's chairman, president and chief executive officer in a news release. "We will continue to pursue all judicial and administrative remedies available to us to rectify the harm imposed on Foster Wheeler, the Village of Robbins, and the investors in the project by the unlawful partial repeal of the Retail Rate Law."
In 1994, Robbins sold $320 million of tax-exempt, unrated revenue bonds to finance the waste-to-energy incinerator. Last month, a tender of nearly all of the bonds was completed.

The tender resulted in the exchange of the 1994 bonds for restructured bonds that featured a lower interest rate, some extended maturities, additional credit support from Foster Wheeler, new convenants and different redemption provisions.

Robinson had no comment on Foster Wheeler's announcement that it would appeal the dismissal in the U.S. Court of Appeals and is considering refiling its lawsuit in state court. The Clinton, N.J.-based company also said it will consider pursuing administrative remedies with the Illinois Commerce Commission.
